title: Dynamic shape handling: padding, bucketing, and kernel selection (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a pragmatic, incremental design for handling variable input sequence lengths in the serving runtime. Goals are to minimize wasted compute/memory from padding, keep latency predictable under SLOs, and pick the most efficient kernel on a per-batch or per-shape basis while preserving KV-cache correctness and memory safety.

Scope and constraints:
- Models: decoder-only and encoder-decoder families (broad coverage but focus on transformer decoder workloads we serve most).
- Hardware: GPU pools with mixed device generations, including A100/RTX/other AVC; quantized runtimes included.
- Backwards compatibility: Must not break existing API/rollouts; changes behind flags and per-model config.

Design overview (high-level):
1) Shape fingerprinting + short-lifetime aggregation: record a compact fingerprint for incoming request shapes (sequence length, context length, dtype, top-k sampling flags). Maintain an in-memory histogram of recent shapes per model endpoint (sliding-window, 5min).

2) Bucketing policies: hybrid approach with two layers:
   - Static seed buckets (config per model): a small set of commonly useful lengths (e.g., [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]). Useful to cover common app tiers.
   - Dynamic quantile buckets: compute lightweight quantiles over the 5min shape histogram and create buckets at p10/p30/p60/p90 to capture real traffic skew. Recompute every minute with exponential decay to adapt to bursts.

3) Padding policies (policy enum and runtime effect):
   - NONE (per-request kernel): no padding; execute each request independently. Lowest padding cost but lowest batching efficiency. Useful for low-concurrency or strict single-request latency SLOs.
   - PER-BUCKET (bucket-level padding): pad all requests in a batch to the bucket target length. This is the default for throughput-oriented dedicated pools.
   - ADAPTIVE_TRIM (experimental): when a batch contains many long sequences and a few extremely short ones, trim short tokens for this batch with a best-effort restore using KV-cache placeholders (see KV cache section).
   - PREFIX_PAD (for prompts with long shared prefixes): detect identical prefixes and reuse prefix KV cache; only pad/generate on suffix lengths.

4) Kernel selection and registry:
   - Runtime maintains a kernel registry keyed by (model-arch, device-capability, dtype, padded-seq-len). Each entry contains a profile: throughput (tokens/s), peak-memory, warmup-cost.
   - When forming a batch for a bucket, choose the kernel with the best expected cost per token under current device load. Cost = latency_penalty + alpha*(1/throughput) + beta*(memory_headroom_penalty). alpha/beta tunable per cluster.
   - Fall-back rules: if a bucket kernel is unavailable (e.g., warmup not done), use adjacent smaller kernel and accept some performance loss, or if memory insufficient, split the batch.

5) Scheduler integration (continuous batching + latency SLOs):
   - Batcher considers (arrival time, deadline derived from SLO, shape bucket). Max-wait per bucket is a function of target latency percentile; smaller buckets for latency-sensitive customers get lower max-wait.
   - Slack-window batching: allow flexible mixing of near sizes within a small window (e.g., +/- 10%) to improve fill while bounding padding overhead.
   - QoS tiers: allow route-level override of padding policy (e.g., deferrable work uses PER-BUCKET, interactive routes use NONE or small-bucket PER-BUCKET).

6) KV cache interactions:
   - Key principle: KV cache entries are keyed by request id and absolute position. Bucketing/padding must preserve the semantics of absolute token positions.
   - For ADAPTIVE_TRIM, we insert synthetic placeholders for trimmed tokens into the per-request cache so that subsequent generation indexes map correctly; this adds bookkeeping but avoids full-padding cost. Placeholders are small metadata entries and do not consume full KV memory.
   - Eviction: prefer evicting placeholder entries first. Eviction strategy remains LRU with a per-model soft quota.
   - Shared-prefix optimization: if multiple requests share identical prefix tokens (verified via fast hash), serve prefix KLUT (key lookup table) once and point subsequent requests to that cached prefix. This reduces repeated prefix computation and makes prefix-padding cheap.

Telemetry and metrics to collect (must land in runtime dashboards):
- Per-bucket: request_count, average_padding_ratio, tokens_generated_per_sec, kernel_used, memory_headroom, queue_time, service_time
- Per-model: histogram of sequence lengths (live), fraction of requests using ADAPTIVE_TRIM, prefix-shared hit rate, KV-cache placeholder rate, eviction rate
- Per-kernel: warmup_time, avg_throughput, failure_count (OOM or kernel-mismatch)

Experiments & microbenchmarks (planned):
- Baseline: naive global padding to max in-batch length vs. PER-BUCKET with static seeds vs. PER-BUCKET with dynamic quantiles. Measure tokens/s, tail latency (p95/p99), and memory.
- ADAPTIVE_TRIM correctness microtests: ensure generated token sequences are equivalent to full-pad baseline for a representative prompt corpus.
- Kernel selection heuristics A/B: test alpha/beta weighting under varying contention to find robust defaults.

Operational roll-out plan (staged):
1) Canary: enable per-model telemetry and offline bucket suggestion tool. No runtime enforcement, only recommendations to model owners.
2) Beta: enable PER-BUCKET (static seeds) on dedicated clusters behind a flag. Collect metrics and failures.
3) Production: enable dynamic quantile buckets + kernel selection heuristics for eligible models and device types. ADAPTIVE_TRIM remains experimental behind feature flag.

API and config surface (proposal snippets):
- model.config.padding_policy: [NONE|PER_BUCKET|ADAPTIVE_TRIM|PREFIX_PAD]
- model.config.static_buckets: [32,64,128,256]
- model.config.latency_slo_ms: 150
- runtime.cluster.alpha_beta: ["0.6,0.4"] (internal only)

Open questions and trade-offs:
- Placeholder correctness vs. memory saving: placeholders simplify trimming but increase complexity in eviction and debugging. Is the operational cost worth the memory win?
- Granularity of buckets: too many increases kernel permutations and warmup time; too few increases padding waste. How many is optimal per device class?
- Kernel warmup strategy: eager warmup for popular buckets vs. on-demand. Eager reduces latency but wastes GPU cycles. We need heuristics tied to observed bucket frequency.
- Side-effects on tracing: when trimming/prefix-reuse occurs, how do we reflect this in user-visible trace logs without overwhelming the UI?

Appendix: heuristics and formulas (informal)
- bucket_cost_estimate(bucket) = (1/throughput_est(bucket)) * expected_tokens_in_batch + warmup_penalty
- effective_padding_ratio = sum((padded_len - actual_len)/padded_len for each req)/N
- max_wait_for_bucket(b) = base_wait * (1 - min(0.5, bucket_fill_rate)) with clamp to [2ms, 200ms]

Action items (owners):
- Priya: implement shape fingerprinting + histogram (due 2024-06-03)
- Mateo: prototype dynamic quantile bucketer as a standalone binary (due 2024-06-10)
- Evelyn: add kernel registry proto + perf profiling harness (due 2024-06-17)
- Samir: KV-cache placeholder prototype and correctness tests (due 2024-06-24)
- Janelle: telemetry dashboards + alerts for padding_ratio > 0.25 (due 2024-06-14)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we prefer an incremental feature set that is toggleable per-model. Please call out missing safety checks or interactions with routing/fallbacks you think are risky.
- If you have prior perf traces that show clear bucket boundaries for common customers, paste them in GH:repo/runtime#842 or link in comments.
